summary: For ages 9–10: generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule, then notice a feature the rule did NOT state (alternating odd/even, all-even, a repeating units-digit cycle) and explain informally WHY it must continue from the rule's structure. The teaching goal is to move from spotting a feature to justifying it (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), using a term-number vs value table and growing shape pictures to seed position-to-term thinking.
misconceptions: Applying the rule inconsistently or miscounting steps when generating terms.
'Explaining' a feature by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Assuming a short-run feature always holds without justification (over-generalising).
Confusing the term-to-term rule with a position-to-term rule.
Not distinguishing the starting number's role from the step's role in an emergent feature.

activities.title: Generate, then colour by parity to spot a hidden feature
steps: Take the rule 'start at 1, add 3' and write the first eight terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22.
Mark each 'add 3' jump between consecutive terms (on a number line or by an arrow) so the step stays constant.
Colour or mark each term as odd or even and describe what you notice about the sequence of colours.
Record each term in a table with two columns: term number (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and value, so emergent features line up next to their positions.
Predict whether the 10th term will be odd or even, then generate it and check.
activities.insight: A rule states a step, but the generated sequence can show a feature the rule never mentioned — here the terms strictly alternate odd, even, odd, even — and a table or parity colouring makes that feature visible.

activities.title: Explain WHY the feature must continue
steps: For 'start at 1, add 3', explain why the odd/even labels keep alternating: adding 3 (an odd number) flips parity every single time, so the alternation must continue forever, not just for the terms you wrote.
For 'start at 2, add 4', predict before writing whether every term will be even, then justify: starting even and adding an even number keeps the result even, because even + even = even.
State a prediction for a step of 2 instead of 3 and explain how the parity pattern would differ (adding an even number leaves parity unchanged).
Give a structural reason, not just a restatement: say WHY it happens from the rule, not merely THAT it happens.
activities.insight: An emergent feature can be justified from the structure of the rule: an odd step makes the terms alternate (and the starting number fixes which parity the alternation begins with), while an even step keeps every term the same parity (and the start fixes that parity). So the feature must hold for all terms, not just the observed ones.

activities.title: Vary the step to discover the roles of start and step
steps: Keep the start fixed and change the step from 3 (odd) to 4 (even); generate both sequences and compare the parity colouring — alternating for the odd step, locked for the even step.
Now keep the step fixed and change the starting number; notice which feature changes (which parity the terms begin with) and which stays the same (whether they alternate).

Articulate the two distinct roles you discovered: the step's parity decides whether the terms alternate (odd step) or stay a single fixed parity (even step); the start fixes which parity the sequence begins with — the one it stays on for an even step, or the one it starts the alternation with for an odd step.
Test a prediction before computing: for a new rule, say what the hidden feature will be and why, then generate terms to confirm.
activities.insight: The starting number and the step play different roles in an emergent feature; experimenting by changing one at a time isolates each role.

activities.title: Growing shape patterns and position-to-term
steps: Continue a growing dot or tile pattern by predicting the next three terms and describing the rule in words.
Count the dots/tiles in each stage and record stage number next to the count in a two-column table.
Link the stage (term) number to its count, and predict a later stage's count, explaining how you used the position rather than drawing every stage.
Notice any hidden feature in the counts (e.g. always even, or a repeating units digit) and explain it from how the shape grows each step.
activities.insight: Growing shape patterns connect the term number to a count, seeding position-to-term (nth-term) thinking and giving a concrete picture of an emergent numeric feature.

activities.title: Pattern-detective discussion: justify the feature aloud
steps: With a partner or adult playing a 'pattern detective', state a feature you noticed and be ready to defend it.
The detective accepts the feature ONLY when you give a structural reason for why it continues (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), not when you restate the observation.

Answer probing questions such as: 'Besides adding 3, what pattern do you see in the numbers?', 'Why do the terms of start-at-2-add-4 stay even?', 'If you start at 1 and add 3, would 30 ever appear — how can you tell?', and 'What changes if the step is 2 instead of 3?'
Revise your explanation if it's only a restatement until it names the structural cause.
activities.insight: Explaining informally means giving a reason rooted in the rule's structure that shows a feature must persist, not merely reporting what you saw.

checkQuestion: Give the child a rule and watch them generate and analyse the pattern: 'Start at 1 and keep adding 3 — write the first eight terms.' Then ask: 'What do you notice about the pattern that the rule didn't tell you?' Then give 'start at 2, add 4' and ask them to predict, before writing, whether all the terms will be even and why. Watch the term generation and the informal explanation of a hidden feature.
checkAnswer: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 — the child should notice a feature not in the rule, e.g. the terms alternate odd, even, odd, even, or the ones-digits cycle 1,4,7,0,3,6,9,2. For 'start at 2, add 4': all terms even, because starting even and adding an even number keeps it even. The teacher watches for correct generation AND an informal 'why' for a spotted feature.
